discovery_articles.title: The Tiffany Dome at Chateau Big Bear Boutique Hotel in Big Bear Lake, California
discovery_articles.snippet: In a ski town two hours from Los Angeles, in a bistro serving cocktails and bar snacks, hangs the largest Tiffany-style stained-glass dome west of Chicago — and it didn't start out anywhere near a mountain. The 57-foot dome was originally installed in a Parisian tango house during the city's so-called "Golden Age of Brothels," a period when clandestine dance halls and pleasure houses commissioned lavish decorative glasswork to match their reputations. At some point after that chapter closed, the dome was carefully disassembled panel by panel and shipped across the Atlantic, eventually finding its way to Chateau Big Bear, a French-inspired hotel built in 1987 in the San Bernardino National Forest.

discovery_articles.title: Bear Rocks Preserve in Davis, West Virginia
discovery_articles.snippet: Perched more than 4,000 feet above sea level at the northern edge of Dolly Sods, Bear Rocks is one of the most unusual landscapes in the Appalachian Mountains. Its broad sandstone outcrops overlook the Allegheny Front, while stunted red spruce, blueberry and huckleberry heath, and open barrens create an ecosystem more commonly associated with Canada than West Virginia. The combination of elevation, exposure, and cool climate has allowed northern plant communities to persist here long after the last Ice Age retreated.

featured_read.title: How to Hold the Darkness: Notes on Living Through Uncertainty
featured_read.snippet: There are times in life when the continent of certainty parts underfoot and, as the ash cloud of the old world rains darkness upon us, we are asked to swim in the rivers of lava that will make the new. “Almost it would appear that it is useless in such confusion to ask,” wrote Virginia Woolf of such times, “those questions as to what, and why, and wherefore.” Unlike her staunchly secularized contemporaries, who shuddered to speak of the soul for fear of being seen as anti-intellectual, Woolf devoted her life to communicating from and with “all these wayward parts… read article
featured_read.blurb: This essay sits with Virginia Woolf's conviction that the soul is not a retreat from reason but the only instrument precise enough to navigate genuine uncertainty. It asks what it actually means to hold — not resolve — the darkness when the ground beneath you stops being solid.
